The reason is that the doors those kind of walk-in freezers/refrigerators are all built with mechanisms that are supposed to allow someone potentially trapped inside to escape even if the door is locked from the outside. On all the models I've worked with there was a way to basically remove the door handle and/or latch from the inside, allowing the door to open. The article says that this freezer did have that sort of safety feature in place, but it malfunctioned somehow.
Why can't they just have a doorknob like a regular door? And even if they don't have a knob, why can't they just be pushed open like a refrigerator door? Thanks.

All the ones I've ever worked with could just be pushed open from the inside. Without knowing more about the particular door they used on the freezer I can only guess at what went wrong. As for doorknobs, these kinds of doors don't work like that. If you've never seen a walk-in fridge door picture something more along the lines of a bank vault door than your front door. These things are big and in most cases very heavy. I'm not an engineer, but the reason seems to be to keep a good seal on the doorway. They also have to be large so that racks or sometimes even pallets of food/groceries can go in and out of them easily. I worked in a buffet in a major hotel/casino in Atlantic City several years ago and the main walk-in and freezer combined was bigger than my current apartment. We would literally take pallets of food from the loading dock directly into the fridge.Then there was the banquet/long-term freezer. That thing was mammoth. It was the size of a small house and had a set of side-rolling doors like on an airplane hangar. Next to it were the two banquet refrigerators which were the size of garages, and had reticulated garage doors.

My best guess at how this happened is that the door on the freezer has some sort of latch that got stuck and the woman couldn't push the door open, or even worse someone locked the door from the outside and didn't know she was in there. Not all walk-in doors I've seen had windows on them. Add in that they found the emergency release on the door to be faulty and this poor woman ends up a Popsicle.

Time-boxing: breaking the day up into segments to track/designate how you spend your time.
I recently started time boxing my day. So my phone will alert me when it's time to do anything. I've been liking it so far, but I'm not super strict with it as life changes day to day.

What sort of time increments do you use?
Nothing less than an hour. Just saying this hour is for this task. Clean between these hours, study between these, etc. Then if this change I have to decide what time slot to steal from, starting with the non-productive time boxes.

What sorts of tasks do you assign per chunk of time?
Nothing too specific. Just break up my day into chunks. Wake up, breakfast/shower get ready for the day, cleaning time, lunch, coding/study time, cook/eat drinner, workout, and then enjoy the rest of my evening assuming I've been keeping on my schedule and productive.
